hints: Think about which O-H bond is easier to break, the one in water or the one in ethanol, and what that tells you about acidity.
Remember that sodium fizzes much more violently with water than with ethanol, so water must be the stronger acid here.
Link acid strength to base strength of the conjugate base, and consider how the ethyl group pushes electron density toward the oxygen.
walkthrough:
**Compare the reactivity with sodium**

Think of what you see in the lab. Sodium reacts violently with water but much more gently with ethanol.

This tells us water loses its $\text{H}^+$ more easily, so water is more acidic than ethanol.

**Link acidity to basicity of the conjugate base**

A useful rule is: the weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \text{ (weaker acid)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^- \text{ (stronger base)}$$
$$\text{H}_2\text{O} \text{ (stronger acid)} \rightarrow \text{OH}^- \text{ (weaker base)}$$

**Explain with the inductive effect**

The ethyl group, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-$, is electron-donating by the positive inductive (+I) effect.

It pushes electron density onto the already negative oxygen in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$, intensifying the charge and making it more keen to accept a proton, so ethoxide is a stronger base than hydroxide.

options.A: Incorrect. Water is more acidic and reacts faster with sodium than ethanol does. The reaction $2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2$ is vigorous, while $2\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2$ is much slower at the same temperature.
options.B: Correct. Ethanol is a weaker acid than water, so its conjugate base $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$ is stronger than $\text{OH}^-$. The ethyl group donates electrons (+I effect), increasing electron density on oxygen and making ethoxide more able to accept $\text{H}^+$.
options.C: Incorrect. There is no pi system or adjacent p-orbital for the lone pairs to spread into. The negative charge in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$ is localised on the oxygen atom, unlike in carboxylate or phenoxide ions where delocalisation does occur.
options.D: Incorrect. It is harder, not easier, to deprotonate ethanol. Ethanol is less acidic than water because the electron-donating ethyl group destabilises the ethoxide anion relative to hydroxide, so the O-H bond in ethanol is less willing to release $\text{H}^+$.
